[BUG] cuDF: shared-alias multi-pattern with relationship-property projection segfaults (exit 139)
## Summary

On cuDF (rapids 25.02 + 26.02), a Cypher query with shared aliases across comma-separated MATCH patterns and a relationship-property projection in RETURN crashes the Python process (SIGSEGV / exit 139).

## Repro (rapids 25.02 / 26.02 GPU container)

```python
import pandas as pd, graphistry, cudf
graphistry.register(api=3, server="hub.graphistry.com")

nodes = pd.DataFrame({"id":["a1","b1"],"label__A":[True,False],"label__B":[False,True]})
edges = pd.DataFrame({"s":["a1","b1"],"d":["b1","a1"],"type":["R","S"],"weight":[7,9]})
g = (graphistry.nodes(cudf.from_pandas(nodes),"id")
     .edges(cudf.from_pandas(edges),"s","d")
     .bind(edge_label="type"))

# Both of the following segfault with EXIT=139:

# A) WITH-form (goes through flatten path from #1341):
g.gfql(
    "MATCH (a:A {id: 'a1'})-[r:R]->(b:B) "
    "WITH a, b, r "
    "MATCH (b)-[:S]->(a) "
    "RETURN r.weight AS w",
    engine="cudf",
)

# B) Hand-flattened single-MATCH (does NOT go through flatten):
g.gfql(
    "MATCH (a:A {id: 'a1'})-[r:R]->(b:B), (b)-[:S]->(a) "
    "RETURN r.weight AS w",
    engine="cudf",
)
```

Both crash. Pandas equivalent works correctly and returns `[{'w': 7}]`.

## Suspected cause

cuDF row-pipeline shared-alias join with relationship-property projection — likely a C-level interop issue in cudf merge / pylibcudf. Stack trace dumps come from `_PyRun_SimpleFileObject` with `pylibcudf.*` extension modules loaded.

The issue is NOT specific to the new `flatten_carried_endpoint_rebind` path from #1341 — it reproduces equally on the hand-flattened single-MATCH form, so the cuDF bug is in shared-alias multi-pattern join with rel-property projection regardless of how the query reaches it.

## Acceptance criteria

- The repro queries above execute without crashing on cuDF (rapids 25.02 + 26.02).
- Result rows match the pandas baseline (`[{'w': 7}]`).
- New parametrized test under `graphistry/tests/compute/gfql/cypher/test_lowering.py` covering shared-alias multi-pattern + rel-property projection on both engines.

## Surfaced by

PR #1351 (#1341) test-amplification round-001. The corresponding cuDF parity test (`test_string_cypher_executes_with_match_reentry_relationship_variable_carried_on_cudf`) is currently `@pytest.mark.skip`'d with this issue as the link.

Feature request: improve support for parameter injection
### Why is this needed?

My apologies if there something already exists that addresses this issue. I searched all of the code and I just could not figure out a reusable way to handle parameter injection without rolling my own system. 

Request body and query string parsing as well as other aspects of request parsing are not reusable. For example, a pydantic based parameter injection system can be put in place at some point in the stack to make it more reusable. I've implemented this in a work project using a custom decorator

```python
from functools import wraps
from typing import Optional, Type
import inspect
import json

from aws_lambda_powertools.utilities.data_classes import APIGatewayProxyEvent
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

from lib.common.app import app

# NOTE: this utility does not map these types to the open api specification. 
def inject_params(
    query_model: Optional[Type[BaseModel]] = None,
    body_model: Optional[Type[BaseModel]] = None,
):
    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            _ = args
            api_event: APIGatewayProxyEvent = app.current_event
            query_params = None
            body_params = None

            if query_model:
                query_dict = api_event.query_string_parameters or {}
                try:
                    query_params = query_model(**query_dict)
                except ValidationError as e:
                    # Raise validation error to be handled by existing middleware
                    raise e

            if body_model:
                try:
                    body_dict = json.loads(api_event.body or "{}")
                    body_params = body_model(**body_dict)
                except (ValidationError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
                    # Raise validation error to be handled by existing middleware
                    raise e

            # Dynamically inject only the parameters that the handler expects
            handler_sig = inspect.signature(func)
            if "query_params" in handler_sig.parameters and query_params is not None:
                kwargs["query_params"] = query_params
            if "body_params" in handler_sig.parameters and body_params is not None:
                kwargs["body_params"] = body_params

            return func(*args, **kwargs)

        return wrapper

    return decorator
```

Example usage:


```python

from http import HTTPStatus

from get_things import get_things
from lib.common.api_client.models.responses import PaginatedThingResponse
from lib.common.app import app, logger, metrics
from lib.common.aws import JsonResponse # custom class I implemented, ignore for the scope of this issue
from lib.common.dtos import GetThingsRequest
from lib.common.middleware.inject_params import inject_params
from lib.common.utils import run_async


@app.get("/thing")
@inject_params(query_model=GetThingsRequest)
def handler(
    query_params: GetThingsRequest,
) -> JsonResponse[PaginatedThingResponse]:
    response: PaginatedThingResponse = run_async(get_things, query_params)
    return JsonResponse(response, status_code=HTTPStatus.OK)
```


So this allows for reusable request parsing with pydantic.  The documented parsing strategy at this time is something that otherwise has to be repeated in every handler. Since this framework really leans into pydantic already I think this kind of functionality should exist. My implementation doesn't cover header parsing or anything else, but it could be extended to support it. 

I'd be happy to make an open source contribution if it makes sense. If so, where would be the best place?

kimi-cli fixed context length
kimi-cli's `max_context_size: 131072` is set to fixed, but is outdated. The new `kimi-k2.5` supports 256k context window: https://platform.moonshot.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k2-5-quickstart#ultra-long-context-support.

A change could follow the Terminus 2 pattern: accept an optional `model_info` dict kwarg, register it with `litellm.register_model()` if provided, then use `litellm.utils.get_model_info()` to resolve the model's `max_input_tokens` at config-build time. Priority: `model_info` registration (makes LiteLLM lookup succeed for custom models) > LiteLLM database lookup > hardcoded default (131072).

## Summary  
The `kimi-cli` component in the Harbor framework uses a hardcoded `max_context_size=131072` (128k) tokens, which is incompatible with the newer `kimi-k2.5` model that supports up to 256k tokens. This discrepancy prevents users from leveraging the full capabilities of the updated model. The fix should adopt a dynamic model info registration pattern similar to Terminus 2, prioritizing custom model configurations over hardcoded defaults.

## Steps to Reproduce  
1. Initialize `kimi-cli` with the `kimi-k2.5` model  
2. Check the effective `max_context_size` value in the configuration  
3. Observe that the context limit remains at 131072 instead of 256k  

## Expected Behavior  
When using `kimi-k2.5`, the CLI should:  
- Dynamically detect the 256k context window from model metadata  
- Prioritize custom `model_info` registrations over hardcoded defaults  
- Use LiteLLM's `get_model_info()` to resolve context limits at runtime  

## Actual Behavior  
- The hardcoded `max_context_size=131072` is enforced regardless of model version  
- LiteLLM falls back to default values instead of using the 256k limit from [Moonshot's documentation](https://platform.moonshot.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k2-5-quickstart#ultra-long-context-support)  
- Custom model configurations are not properly registered via `litellm.register_model()`

## Summary
The Cypher parser currently rejects zero-hop open-range variable-length relationship syntax like `*0..`, which is needed for official `LDBC SNB Interactive IS2`-style queries.

Environment used for repro:
- repo: `graphistry/pygraphistry`
- sha: `ebe7d0ae827d724a8779e123c3965ec723581015`
- host runtime: `uv run python ...`

## Minimal repro
```python
import pandas as pd
from graphistry.tests.test_compute import CGFull

g = CGFull().nodes(
    pd.DataFrame({
        'id': ['message', 'post'],
        'label__Message': [True, False],
        'label__Post': [False, True],
    }),
    'id',
).edges(
    pd.DataFrame({
        's': ['message'],
        'd': ['post'],
        'type': ['REPLY_OF'],
    }),
    's',
    'd',
)

query = "MATCH (message:Message)-[:REPLY_OF*0..]->(post:Post) RETURN post.id AS postId"
print(g.gfql(query)._nodes)
```

## Observed behavior
This fails with:

```text
GFQLSyntaxError [invalid-cypher-syntax] Invalid Cypher query syntax
```

## Expected behavior
Either:
1. parse and execute `*0..` as standard zero-or-more syntax, or
2. fail fast with an explicit validation error that this syntax is intentionally unsupported.

Right now it looks like a parser-level syntax rejection.

## Why this matters
`SNB IS2` uses `REPLY_OF*0..` so the same pattern can match either:
- a post directly, or
- a comment chain that eventually reaches a post

Without `*0..`, the official query text cannot be expressed directly.

## Related
`#973` explicitly leaves `*0` / `*0..n` out of scope. This issue tracks that specific gap separately.

## Status

Still open as of April 2, 2026.

This remains the active `interactive-short-7` / OPTIONAL MATCH lane.

Related landed work:
- [#1016](https://github.com/graphistry/pygraphistry/pull/1016) fixed the separate `#880` open-range bindings replay bug.
- [#1018](https://github.com/graphistry/pygraphistry/pull/1018) added follow-on amplification and DRY cleanup around that same `#880` replay boundary.
- The `#880` residual bindings-table lane is now considered done and should not be treated as remaining scope for this issue.

## Summary

Direct Cypher execution currently rejects `MATCH ... OPTIONAL MATCH ... RETURN CASE ...` reply-author flag queries with:

`[unsupported-cypher-query] Only node-only pre-binding MATCH clauses are supported before the final connected MATCH in this phase`

This is now a measured benchmark blocker from `pyg-bench` for LDBC SNB Interactive `interactive-short-7` / `IS7`.

## Repro Shape

```cypher
MATCH (m:Message {id: $messageId })<-[:REPLY_OF]-(c:Comment)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(p:Person)
OPTIONAL MATCH (m)-[:HAS_CREATOR]->(a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]-(p)
RETURN c.id AS commentId,
    c.content AS commentContent,
    c.creationDate AS commentCreationDate,
    p.id AS replyAuthorId,
    p.firstName AS replyAuthorFirstName,
    p.lastName AS replyAuthorLastName,
    CASE r
        WHEN null THEN false
        ELSE true
    END AS replyAuthorKnowsOriginalMessageAuthor
ORDER BY commentCreationDate DESC, replyAuthorId
```

## Actual

Compiler/runtime rejects the query before execution with:

```text
[unsupported-cypher-query] Only node-only pre-binding MATCH clauses are supported before the final connected MATCH in this phase
```

## Expected

The query should lower and execute, preserving row semantics for the connected reply rows while null-extending the optional `KNOWS` binding for the boolean flag.

## Benchmark Impact

- blocks direct Cypher coverage for SNB Interactive `interactive-short-7`
- this is the first measured query in our translation queue that clearly requires `OPTIONAL MATCH` + `CASE` semantics rather than only the already-known row/materialization gaps

## Relationship To Existing Issues

- likely related to the broader row-carrier / seeded-row architecture work in `#989`
- distinct from `#981`, which covers multi-binding projection problems after lowering/execution begins
- distinct from `#994`, which is an undirected peer-binding wrong-answer bug on a query that already executes
- distinct from `#880`, which covered the residual bindings-table / replay lane and is now closed after `#1016` and `#1018`

We've confirmed with other clients like TopCat and those do in fact display the table rows. Upon some quick investigation into how astropy is parsing BINARY2 tables, what seems to be happening is that the binary2 converting process handles bounded variable-length char fields by stripping the asterisk in arraysize="128*" and treating it as a fixed-length field, causing it to attempt reading 128 bytes. Specifically, the string fields end up using their Char Converter, where the * is stripped from the arraysize and then astropy switches the binary parsing method to `_binparse_fixed`. This method reads fixed-length arrays by reading a fixed number of bytes (specified by self.arraysize) which seems incorrect for this field type. work around `tempfile` silently ignoring `TMPDIR` if the dir doesn't exist
This should help a lot of users running into `No space left on device` while using `datasets`. Normally the issue is is that `/tmp` is too small and the user needs to use another path, which they would normally set as `export TMPDIR=/some/big/storage`

However, the `tempfile` facility that `datasets` and `pyarrow` use is somewhat broken. If the path doesn't exist it'd ignore it and fall back to using `/tmp`. Watch this:

```
$ export TMPDIR='/tmp/username' 

$ python -c "\
import os
import tempfile
print(os.environ['TMPDIR'])
print(tempfile.gettempdir())"
/tmp/username
/tmp
```

Now let's ensure the path exists:
```
$ export TMPDIR='/tmp/username' 
$ mkdir -p $TMPDIR
$ python -c "\
import os
import tempfile
print(os.environ['TMPDIR'])
print(tempfile.gettempdir())"
/tmp/username
/tmp/username
```

So I recommend `datasets` do either of the 2:
1. assert if `$TMPDIR` dir doesn't exist, telling the user to create it
2. auto-create it

The reason for (1) is that I don't know why `tempdir` doesn't auto-create the dir - perhaps some security implication? I will let you guys make the decision, but the key is not to let things silently fall through and the user puzzling why no matter what they do they can't break past `No space left on device` while using `datasets`

Thank you.

I found this via https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37229398/python-tempfile-gettempdir-does-not-respect-tmpdir while trying to help a colleague to solve this exact issue.

## Summary

The Python `tempfile` module does not create the directory specified by the `TMPDIR` environment variable if it doesn't exist, leading to silent fallback to `/tmp`. This behavior causes unexpected "No space left on device" errors in the `datasets` library when users attempt to override the default temporary directory to avoid small `/tmp` partitions. The issue affects both `datasets` and its dependencies like `pyarrow`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set `TMPDIR` to a non-existent directory:
   ```bash
   export TMPDIR='/tmp/username'
   ```
2. Run a Python script to check `tempfile.gettempdir()`:
   ```python
   import os
   import tempfile
   print(os.environ['TMPDIR'])
   print(tempfile.gettempdir())
   ```
3. Observe output:
   ```
   /tmp/username
   /tmp
   ```
4. Create the directory and repeat:
   ```bash
   mkdir -p $TMPDIR
   ```
   Output becomes:
   ```
   /tmp/username
   /tmp/username
   ```

## Expected Behavior

When `TMPDIR` is set, `tempfile.gettempdir()` should:
- Validate the directory exists, or
- Create it automatically if permissions allow.

This ensures user-configured temporary directories are respected without requiring manual directory creation.

## Actual Behavior

`tempfile.gettempdir()` silently ignores non-existent `TMPDIR` values and falls back to `/tmp`. This breaks user workflows where `/tmp` has limited space, and users expect `TMPDIR` to override this behavior.

## Scope / Affected Areas

- `datasets` library (temp file handling during data loading)
- `pyarrow` (underlying tempfile usage)
- Any code relying on `tempfile` with custom `TMPDIR` configurations

Proposed solutions:
- Add validation/assertion that `TMPDIR` exists before use
- Implement automatic directory creation with appropriate permissions
- Add clear error messaging when `TMPDIR` is invalid

Environment:
- Python 3.x (tested with 3.8+)
- Linux-based systems (common in HPC/cloud environments with restricted `/tmp`)
- `datasets` versions using default `tempfile` behavior

Cypher: relationship alias unsupported in row expression select (blocks IC11 job-referral)
## Summary

When an IC11-style Cypher query uses a relationship alias (e.g. `workAt`) in a `select` row expression, the engine raises an unsupported-token error. This blocks execution of LDBC SNB Interactive Complex Query 11 (IC11 — job-referral).

## Error

```
[invalid-node-reference] Error executing 'select': unsupported token in row expression: 'workAt' | field: function | value: 'select'
```

## Failing Pattern

IC11 matches a friend-of-friend to a company via a `WORKS_AT` relationship and then projects properties from both the relationship (`workAt`) and the company node:

```cypher
MATCH (p:Person {id: $personId})-[:KNOWS*1..2]-(friend:Person),
      (friend)-[workAt:WORKS_AT]->(company:Company)
WHERE workAt.workFrom < $workFromYear
  AND (company)-[:IS_LOCATED_IN]->(:Place {name: $countryName})
RETURN friend.id, friend.firstName, friend.lastName,
       company.name AS organizationName,
       workAt.workFrom AS organizationWorkFromYear
ORDER BY organizationWorkFromYear ASC, friend.lastName ASC, friend.id ASC
LIMIT 10
```

The `workAt` relationship alias appears in the `RETURN` projection, and the engine's `select` row expression evaluator does not handle relationship aliases — only node aliases are supported.

## Relationship to Related Issues

- **#982** (closed) tracked edge alias properties after traversal in GFQL AST. The current gap is specifically in the Cypher `select` row expression path, not the GFQL AST path.
- This is a new, untracked gap in the Cypher lowering layer.

## Affected Queries

- LDBC SNB Interactive Complex 11 (`interactive-complex-11.cypher`) — `job-referral` primitive
- Any Cypher query that projects a relationship alias property in RETURN (e.g. `workAt.workFrom`)

## Provenance

Measured and reported from the [pyg-bench](https://github.com/graphistry/pyg-bench) SNB Interactive conformance harness.

1. A test failure in `test_vsa.py` due to tensor shape unpacking errors during VSA backward testing

UnexpectedRowsExpectation unexpected_rows limit
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Currently, when using UnexpectedRowsExpectation or retrieving unexpected rows in Great Expectations (e.g., result_format: COMPLETE with Spark/SQL), the system returns a maximum of 200 unexpected rows. This limit is hardcoded and prevents users from accessing all failing rows in large datasets. For example, if there are 432 failing rows, only 200 are returned. This makes it difficult to fully analyze validation results without writing extra custom queries.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to have a configurable option to increase or remove this limit, such as:
result_format:
  result_format: COMPLETE
  include_unexpected_rows: True
  max_unexpected_rows: -1  # -1 or None for unlimited

This would allow retrieving all unexpected rows directly from Great Expectations validation results, without memory issues or extra workarounds.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Using Spark filters manually after validation to retrieve all failing rows.
Running multiple partial validations with offsets.

Both alternatives require extra code and duplicate work outside of Great Expectations, which is not ideal.

**Additional context**
[Add any other context, screenshots, or code samples about the feature request here.](https://discourse.greatexpectations.io/t/unexpectedrowsexpectation-unexpected-rows-limit/2026)

## Summary  
Great Expectations currently enforces a hardcoded limit of 200 unexpected rows when using `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` or retrieving unexpected rows via `result_format: COMPLETE` in Spark/SQL backends. This restriction prevents users from accessing full validation results in large datasets, requiring manual workarounds to analyze all failing records.

## Steps to Reproduce  
1. Define an `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` (e.g., `expect_column_values_to_be_in_set`) with `result_format: COMPLETE`  
2. Validate a dataset containing >200 unexpected rows  
3. Observe only the first 200 unexpected rows are returned in validation results  

## Expected Behavior  
Users should be able to configure or remove the row limit via parameters like:  
```yaml
result_format:
  result_format: COMPLETE
  include_unexpected_rows: true
  max_unexpected_rows: -1  # -1 or null for unlimited
```
This would return all unexpected rows directly from validation results without requiring external queries.

## Actual Behavior  
The system silently truncates unexpected rows to a maximum of 200, regardless of dataset size. This behavior is hardcoded in the `UnexpectedRowsExpectation` implementation.

## Scope / Affected Areas  
- **Core Components**: `great_expectations.expectations.unexpected_rows_expectation.py`, `great_expectations.expectation.py`  
- **Execution Backends**: Spark and SQL validation workflows  
- **User Impact**: Requires manual post-processing (e.g., Spark filters, paginated queries) to retrieve full results  
- **Proposed Fix**: Add `max_unexpected_rows` parameter to `result_format` configuration

Allow renaming worker ThreadPool's thread_name_prefix from worker parameters
The [distributed ThreadPoolExecutor](https://github.com/dask/distributed/blob/main/distributed/threadpoolexecutor.py#L86-L91) sets the name of each thread based on thread_name_prefix parameter.

The dask worker, by default, passes a fixed name `Dask-Default-Threads` as the `thread_name_prefix` 
[Corresponding code in dask worker which sets name](https://github.com/dask/distributed/blob/main/distributed/worker.py#L663-L666)

Dask's worker parameters only allow [overriding the executor](https://github.com/dask/distributed/blob/main/distributed/worker.py#L380-L388), but since `executor` has to be an instance of some `Executor` (i.e. its a python object), we can't pass this object from outside of python,
for example, when passing "worker json spec" to the `dask spec` command to start a worker.

If we can allow user to override this thread_name_prefix of the default executor, by adding one more parameter in the worker params which accepts a string, that would be useful.

Also on another note, the default name of the worker threadpool, can be derived from the worker's `self.name` attribute itself, rather than always defaulting to `Dask-Default-Threads`

## Summary  
The Dask worker's default `ThreadPoolExecutor` uses a fixed `thread_name_prefix` ("Dask-Default-Threads"), which cannot be customized via worker parameters. This limits visibility and debugging capabilities in multi-worker environments. The proposal is to introduce a configurable parameter to override this prefix, enabling better thread identification and alignment with worker-specific naming conventions.

## Steps to Reproduce  
1. Launch a Dask worker using a JSON specification with `dask spec` (e.g., `dask spec my-worker-spec.json`).  
2. Attempt to set a custom `thread_name_prefix` for the worker's `ThreadPoolExecutor` via worker parameters.  
3. Observe that the prefix remains hardcoded to "Dask-Default-Threads" regardless of configuration attempts.  

## Expected Behavior  
Users should be able to specify a custom `thread_name_prefix` for the worker's `ThreadPoolExecutor` through worker parameters (e.g., `thread_name_prefix="My-Custom-Threads"`). This would allow thread names to reflect worker identities or deployment contexts (e.g., "Worker-A-Threads").  

## Actual Behavior  
The `ThreadPoolExecutor` in `distributed/worker.py` always uses the fixed prefix "Dask-Default-Threads". Worker parameters only allow overriding the executor instance itself, not its configuration. This makes it impossible to customize thread names without modifying the source code.  

## Scope / Affected Areas  
- **Files**:  
  - `distributed/worker.py` (worker parameter handling and executor initialization)  
  - `distributed/threadpoolexecutor.py` (ThreadPoolExecutor configuration)  
- **Components**:  
  - Worker lifecycle and thread management  
  - JSON spec-based worker deployment (e.g., `dask spec`)  
- **Proposed Changes**:  
  - Add a `thread_name_prefix` parameter to worker configuration options.  
  - Update the default prefix logic to use `self.name` (worker identifier) instead of a hardcoded string.

[bug] Workspaces: No propagation of options from profile
### Describe the bug

When trying the new workspace feature I was comparing how well this would fit to streamline our current workflow.

The majority of our package's conanfiles is using custom `generate()` methods assigning cache variables based on the selected options, for example:
```python
def generate(self):
  ...
  tc = CMakeToolchain(self)
  tc.cache_variables["BUILD_CLIENT_TOOLS"] = self.options.build_client_tools
  tc.cache_variables["BUILD_DOCS"] = self.options.get_safe('build_docs', False)
```

For daily development we maintain a collection of profiles defining toolchains and options for the packages as required for the respective platforms.

```plain
[settings]
os=Linux
arch=x86_64
build_type=Release

[options]
pkg_a/*:build_client_tools=True
..
```

EXIF Orientation=0 raises exception with `exifrotate=True` after upgrading from v2.27
While updating an older codebase I ran into an issue in one of my previously working test cases: the input image (which was likely sourced from a stock photo website) contains non-conforming EXIF metadata and the `Orientation` tag is set to 0, which will cause an exception in `imageio.v3.imread` when called with `exifrotate=True` (the legacy plugin sets `exifrotate` to `True` by default, so I also had to add the parameter manually).

In v2.27 this was not a problem since the legacy plugin just skips all of the `if` branches and keeps the original image data in `im` intact:
https://github.com/imageio/imageio/blob/7c00fd94c914b383be0cb29cbe8ba856518c296f/imageio/plugins/pillow_legacy.py#L499-L511

In newer versions, the new Pillow plugin handles EXIF orientation differently:
https://github.com/imageio/imageio/blob/7c00fd94c914b383be0cb29cbe8ba856518c296f/imageio/plugins/pillow.py#L56-L67

If the value of `orientation` is anything other than 1-8, it raises a KeyError. While this is technically correct according to the EXIF standard, apparrently some older/buggy software writes 0 when orientation is unspecified instead of just omitting the tag.

feat(aws): Add IPv6 address support to EC2Instance and NetworkInterface
# Add IPv6 address support to EC2Instance and NetworkInterface schema nodes

## Description

Cartography's EC2 schema currently has no representation of IPv6 addresses assigned to EC2 instances. The AWS `DescribeInstances` API returns IPv6 addresses under `NetworkInterfaces[].Ipv6Addresses[]`, which could be primarily surfaced through the existing `NetworkInterface` node.

**New node type: `EC2Ipv6Address`**

A new `EC2Ipv6Address` node could follow a similar pattern used to `ElasticIPAdress` nodes, using the `Ip` label so `AWSDNSRecord` AAAA records can point to it via the existing `DNS_POINTS_TO` relationship, and be related to the `NetworkInterface` the address is attached to:

```
(AWSDNSRecord)-[DNS_POINTS_TO]->(EC2Ipv6Address)
(NetworkInterface)-[IPV6_ADDRESS]->(EC2Ipv6Address)
```

Fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `ipv6_address` | The IPv6 address |
| `network_interface_id` | The ID of the network interface this address is associated with |
| `primary` | Whether this is the primary IPv6 address on the interface |
| `id` | Same as `ipv6_address` |

**`EC2Instance` node: `ipv6address` field**

Similar to how the primary interface's IPv4 addresses are surfaced in `EC2Instance` the model should be extended to contain the IPv6 address of its primary interface as well for simpler queries. 

## Motivation

Following your gracious and rapid resolution of [my previous request](https://github.com/cartography-cncf/cartography/issues/1945) for Route53 AAAA support (which has been working well, by the way, thank you!), we've now encountered gaps in our ability to correlate DNS records to our EC2 instances since Cartography isn't currently collecting the IPv6 addresses of instances.

Cypher aggregates (collect, count(*), sum) over relationship-pattern rows rejected: runtime collapses rows before aggregation
## Summary

Cypher aggregates (`collect`, `count(*)`, `sum`, etc.) applied over rows produced by a `MATCH` containing a relationship pattern are rejected: the GFQL runtime collapses relationship rows before the aggregate fires, so multiplicity-sensitive aggregation cannot run. This blocks the LDBC SNB IC1 `collect(CASE ...)` shapes for unis / companies and shapes in several other IC* lanes.

## Repros (minimal, both fail on master `41d865ac9`)

**Shape A — `collect(alias.prop)` over OPTIONAL MATCH:**
```cypher
MATCH (p:Person {id: $pid})
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[s:STUDY_AT]->(uni:University)
WITH p, collect(uni.name) AS unis
RETURN p.id AS personId, unis
```

**Shape B — `collect(CASE ...)` over OPTIONAL MATCH (IC1 official):**
```cypher
MATCH (p:Person {id: $pid})
OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[s:STUDY_AT]->(uni:University)
WITH p, collect(CASE uni.name WHEN null THEN null ELSE [uni.name, s.classYear] END) AS unis
RETURN p.id AS personId, unis
```

## Expected vs observed

- Helper: `_reject_unsound_relationship_multiplicity_aggregates` (same file, ~`:2425`)
- Predicate: `_is_multiplicity_sensitive_aggregate`

- IC1 (`results/runs/dgx-spark-ic1-conformance-2026-04-05/`): official query uses `collect(CASE company.name ... END) AS companies` and the unis variant.
- IC4 (`results/runs/dgx-spark-ic4-conformance-2026-04-05/`): partial; sum/count over multi-stage WITH is now mostly cleared by #1057, but `collect()` over relationship rows remains blocked here.

- `graphistry/compute/gfql/row/pipeline.py` (bindings-row aggregate execution path)

## Summary
The GFQL runtime incorrectly collapses relationship-pattern rows before executing aggregation operations, preventing valid Cypher queries that use `collect`, `count(*)`, or `sum` on relationship-based data. This blocks critical LDBC SNB IC1 queries and other benchmarks requiring multiplicity-sensitive aggregation.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Execute the following queries against the GFQL runtime (tested on commit `41d865ac9`):
   - **Shape A**: `collect(alias.prop)` over `OPTIONAL MATCH`
     ```cypher
     MATCH (p:Person {id: $pid})
     OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[s:STUDY_AT]->(uni:University)
     WITH p, collect(uni.name) AS unis
     RETURN p.id AS personId, unis
     ```
   - **Shape B**: `collect(CASE ...)` over `OPTIONAL MATCH` (LDBC IC1 official pattern)
     ```cypher
     MATCH (p:Person {id: $pid})
     OPTIONAL MATCH (p)-[s:STUDY_AT]->(uni:University)
     WITH p, collect(CASE uni.name WHEN null THEN null ELSE [uni.name, s.classYear] END) AS unis
     RETURN p.id AS personId, unis
     ```
2. Observe the `GFQLValidationError` rejecting the query due to premature row collapse.

## Expected Behavior
- Aggregates like `collect(uni.name)` and `collect(CASE ...)` should return per-person collections of all matched relationship data.
- Queries such as `MATCH (a)-[r]->(b) RETURN a, count(*)` should execute without error.

## Actual Behavior
- Queries fail with `GFQLValidationError: [unsupported-cypher-query]` due to the runtime collapsing relationship rows before aggregation.
- The guard `_reject_unsound_relationship_multiplicity_aggregates` in `lowering.py` blocks valid multiplicity-sensitive operations.

## Scope / Affected Areas
- **Core Files**:
  - `graphistry/compute/gfql/cypher/lowering.py` (aggregate dispatch logic, `_reject_unsound_relationship_multiplicity_aggregates` guard)
  - `graphistry/compute/gfql/row/pipeline.py` (aggregate execution path for bindings rows)
- **Key Constraints**:
  - The guard at `lowering.py:2417` must be modified to allow safe multiplicity-sensitive aggregates.
  - Regression tests are required for `collect(alias.prop)`, `collect(CASE ...)`, `count(*)`, and `sum(edge.prop)` patterns.
- **Benchmarks Impacted**:
  - LDBC IC1 (`collect(CASE ...)` for universities/companies)
  - IC4, IC5, IC6, IC7, IC8, IC11, IC12 (various `collect`/`count` patterns)

Make ACE lesson matching opt-in via configuration
## Problem

The ACE (Automated Context Embedding) lesson matching system currently auto-enables when it detects that `sentence-transformers` is installed. This causes issues:

1. **Fragile import detection**: The code tries to import `sentence_transformers` and if available, initializes ACE
2. **Silent failures**: When ACE initialization fails (e.g., missing attributes), it logs warnings but falls back silently
3. **Environment confusion**: In pipx environments, dependencies may or may not be available depending on installation method
4. **Not user-controlled**: Users can't explicitly enable/disable ACE

## Current Behavior

From `gptme/tools/lessons.py`:
- Auto-detects `sentence_transformers` availability
- If available, tries to initialize `LessonEmbedder`
- If initialization fails, logs warning and falls through

This causes logs like:
```
Error: sentence-transformers not installed.
WARNING Error during lesson auto-inclusion: 'LessonEmbedder' object has no attribute '_lesson_to_id'
```

## Proposed Solution

Make ACE opt-in via gptme configuration:

```toml
# gptme.toml
[lessons]
ace_enabled = false  # Explicit opt-in
```

Or via environment variable:
```bash
GPTME_ACE_ENABLED=true gptme
```

Benefits:
- User controls whether to use experimental features
- Clear error messages when explicitly enabled but dependencies missing
- No silent failures in production use
- Clean separation between keyword matching (stable) and ACE (experimental)

## Additional Cleanup

The `lessons.py` import detection could use cleanup:
- Remove fragile try/except import pattern
- Add proper configuration check before attempting ACE
- Clear error messages when configuration doesn't match available dependencies

## Context

This came up during autonomous operation health checks - the lesson system was silently failing every run without clear indication of the issue.

cc @ErikBjare

fix: custom macro parameters not expanded in LaTeX backend
## Description

The LaTeX backend does not expand custom macro parameters (`#1`, `#2`, etc.) when processing user-defined macros via `\newcommand`. This causes unexpanded parameter references and their surrounding formatting commands to leak into the output.

**Example:**
```latex
\newcommand{\highlight}[1]{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{#1}}}
\highlight{Result}
```
produces output containing literal `\textcolor{white}{\textbf{#1}}` or `\textbf{#1}` instead of the substituted text "Result".

Another pattern:
```latex
\newcommand{\metric}[2]{#1{\scriptsize$\_{#2}$}}
```
leaks `\scriptsize` and `#2` references.

## Affected Papers (from testing on 24 arXiv papers)

| Paper | Leaked Commands | Count |
|-------|----------------|-------|
| 2603.25737v1 | `\textbf`, `\small` | 35+12 |
| 2603.25723v1 | `\scriptsize` | 12 |

## Root Cause

When `\newcommand` definitions are encountered, the backend stores the macro body but does not substitute `#1`/`#2`/etc. with actual arguments at expansion time.

## Expected Behavior

Custom macro parameters should be properly substituted with their arguments before the macro body is parsed for formatting commands.

## Context

Discovered during extended testing for PR #3204. See [test report comment](https://github.com/docling-project/docling/pull/3204#issuecomment) for full details.

[BUG] cuDF: length(path) on shortestPath returns object/string dtype instead of numeric
## Summary

On cuDF (rapids 25.02 + 26.02), Cypher `length(path)` projection on a `shortestPath()` alias returns the path-length column as `object`/string dtype (e.g., `'1'`, `'2'`) instead of numeric (`1.0`, `2.0` as on pandas).

## Repro (rapids 25.02 / 26.02 GPU container)

```python
import pandas as pd, graphistry, cudf
graphistry.register(api=3, server="hub.graphistry.com")

nodes = pd.DataFrame({"id":["p1","p2","p3","p4"],"label__Person":[True]*4})
edges = pd.DataFrame({"s":["p1","p2","p1"],"d":["p2","p3","p4"],"type":["KNOWS"]*3})
g = (graphistry.nodes(cudf.from_pandas(nodes),"id")
     .edges(cudf.from_pandas(edges),"s","d")
     .bind(edge_label="type"))

q = """
    MATCH (p:Person {id: 'p1'}), (friend:Person)
    WHERE NOT p = friend
    WITH p, friend
    MATCH path = shortestPath((p)-[:KNOWS*1..3]-(friend))
    RETURN friend.id AS friendId, length(path) AS dist
    ORDER BY friendId
"""
out = g.gfql(q, engine="cudf")
print(out._nodes.dtypes)
# friendId    object
# dist        object   <-- expected numeric
print(out._nodes.to_pandas().to_dict(orient="records"))
# [{'friendId': 'p2', 'dist': '1'}, {'friendId': 'p3', 'dist': '2'}, {'friendId': 'p4', 'dist': '1'}]
```

Pandas returns `dist` as float64. Both the WITH-form (flatten path) and the hand-flattened single-MATCH form produce identical (broken) cuDF output, so the divergence is a cuDF row-pipeline issue, not specific to the new `flatten_carried_endpoint_rebind` path from #1341.

## Suspected cause

`__cypher_shortest_path_hops__path` is populated as Python int per BFS hop in `_gfql_multihop_binding_rows` (`graphistry/compute/gfql/row/pipeline.py:3046`). On cuDF, mixing the int hop values with NaN/None for unreached states likely promotes the column dtype to `object`. Down at projection time `length(path)` resolves to `friend.__cypher_shortest_path_hops__path` (`graphistry/compute/gfql/cypher/ast_normalizer.py:288-291`) and returns the object-typed series as-is.

## Acceptance criteria

- `length(path)` projects a numeric (int64 or float64) dtype on cuDF, parity with pandas.
- New parametrized test under `graphistry/tests/compute/gfql/cypher/test_shortest_path_parity.py` (or analogous) verifying parity on both engines.
- No regression on the pandas path.

## Surfaced by

PR #1351 (#1341) test-amplification round-001. Currently worked around in `test_string_cypher_executes_ic1_shortest_path_with_carried_endpoints_rebound_on_cudf` by int-coercing the assertion.

M4-PR3: implement PredicatePushdownPass rewrite using pass framework + safety primitives
Parent: #1179
Depends on: #1180 (pass framework), #1181 (pushdown safety primitives)

## Objective
Implement the actual `PredicatePushdownPass` logical-plan rewrite now that framework and safety primitives are merged.

## Scope
- Add `PredicatePushdownPass` implementation under `graphistry/compute/gfql/passes/`.
- Rewrite `Filter(input=PatternMatch(...))` by pushing safe predicates into `PatternMatch.predicates`.
- Respect `OPTIONAL MATCH` null-extension semantics via existing safety helpers in `gfql/ir/pushdown_safety.py`.
- Respect `WITH`/ScopeFrame barriers (no pushdown across scope-reset boundaries).
- Keep pass pure (no in-place mutation).

## Acceptance
- Safe predicates are pushed into `PatternMatch.predicates` and residual predicates remain as `Filter` when only partially pushable.
- Null-rejecting predicates on optional-arm aliases are **not** pushed into optional arms.
- WITH-boundary barrier blocks pushdown where required.
- Pass executes through `PassManager` and verifier remains green after pass application.
- No semantic regression in existing Cypher OPTIONAL behavior tests.

## Test Gate
- Unit tests for full-push, partial-push, and no-push cases.
- Negative tests proving optional-arm null-rejecting predicates stay above optional match.
- Boundary tests proving WITH/ScopeFrame blocks backward pushdown.
- Integration test proving logical plan flows through pass manager and produces stable output plan shape.

## Non-goals
- No IndexRewritePass in this issue.
- No broad cost-based optimization work in this issue.
- No physical planner route changes in this issue.

## Notes
- Prefer small deterministic rewrites and explicit plan-shape assertions in tests.
- If discovered edge cases require additional safety helper extensions, track those in this PR scope only when directly required for predicate pushdown correctness.

# Add IPv6 address support to EC2Instance and NetworkInterface schema nodes

## Description

Cartography's EC2 schema currently has no representation of IPv6 addresses assigned to EC2 instances. The AWS `DescribeInstances` API returns IPv6 addresses under `NetworkInterfaces[].Ipv6Addresses[]`, which could be primarily surfaced through the existing `NetworkInterface` node.

(AWSDNSRecord)-[DNS_POINTS_TO]->(EC2Ipv6Address)
(NetworkInterface)-[IPV6_ADDRESS]->(EC2Ipv6Address)

segmentation fault with autoreload due to not updating function __closure__
The code for updating old function references in `IPython/extensions/autoreload.py` is fairly straightforward:
```
func_attrs = [
    "__code__",
    "__defaults__",
    "__doc__",
    "__closure__",
    "__globals__",
    "__dict__",
]


def update_function(old, new):
    """Upgrade the code object of a function"""
    for name in func_attrs:
        try:
            setattr(old, name, getattr(new, name))
        except (AttributeError, TypeError):
            pass
```
But calling setattr on `__closure__` gets `AttributeError('readonly attribute')` so it doesn't actually update it.

We have the following code in reload.py:
```
def decorate(func):
    free_var_y = "y"
    free_var_x = "x"

    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("x is:", free_var_x)
        print("y is:", free_var_y)
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


@decorate
def f():
    return "v1"
```

In IPython we do:
```
In [1]: %load_ext autoreload

In [2]: %autoreload all

In [3]: from reload import f

In [4]: old_f = f

In [5]: old_f()
x is: x
y is: y
Out[5]: 'v1'
```

Now we update reload.py to be:
```
def decorate(func):
    free_var_ay = "ay"
    free_var_bx = "bx"

    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("x is:", free_var_bx)
        print("y is:", free_var_ay)
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


@decorate
def f():
    return "v2"
```
Now the co_freevars of the new code object are in a different order from the old function's `__closure__` attribute so I expected IPython to print the wrong values. But actually now when calling old_f or f again in IPython I get a segmentation fault. Also when a function has changed the number of variables it closes over, as IPython updates `__code__` but not `__closure__`, we will get an error like ValueError('wrapper() requires a code object with 3 free vars, not 6').

I am working on an environment to enable interactive development without restarting python using autoreload, where I addressed this in this commit: https://codeberg.org/sczi/swanky-python/commit/748952d0eda733c7abef5e7e01c1dafdc42e4b43

I just use ctypes.pythonapi.PyFunction_SetClosure which is a CPython only api, as I don't currently have a need for supporting pypy or other implementations. I considered some possibilities that should work on all python implementations:
1) find and update old references with gc.get_referrers
If we update all dict references to use the full new function object, that takes care of top level module references by way of `module.__dict__`, local variables by way of frame.f_locals dict, and class instance variables or methods by way of `class.__dict__`. But we would need special cases to handle classes with slots, and references stored in lists or other container types. But we can't include custom checks for every possible container type, just the containers in the standard library, and we can't update old references in immutable containers like tuples. So it would mostly work but cause occasional bugs by not updating everything properly.
2) use a trampoline function
We could generate a trampoline function with the same number of freevars as the old function object, that just wraps and calls the new version. This would avoid the errors about `ValueError('wrapper() requires a code object with 3 free vars, not 6')`. But it requires wrapping functions which would impact performance and pollute stack traces.

## Summary
The IPython autoreload extension causes segmentation faults when reloading functions with modified closures. This occurs because the `__closure__` attribute of function objects is not updated during autoreload, leading to inconsistencies between the function's code object (`__code__`) and its closure variables. The issue manifests when free variables in closures change order or count between reloads.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a module `reload.py` with a decorator that defines free variables in a closure:
   ```python
   def decorate(func):
       free_var_y = "y"
       free_var_x = "x"
       def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
           print("x is:", free_var_x)
           print("y is:", free_var_y)
           return func(*args, **kwargs)
       return wrapper

   @decorate
   def f():
       return "v1"
   ```
2. In IPython, load the autoreload extension and execute:
   ```python
   %load_ext autoreload
   %autoreload all
   from reload import f
   old_f = f
   old_f()  # Outputs 'v1' with correct closure values
   ```
3. Modify `reload.py` to change free variable names/order and return value:
   ```python
   def decorate(func):
       free_var_ay = "ay"
       free_var_bx = "bx"
       def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
           print("x is:", free_var_bx)
           print("y is:", free_var_ay)
           return func(*args, **kwargs)
       return wrapper

   @decorate
   def f():
       return "v2"
   ```
4. Re-execute `old_f()` or `f()` in IPython. A segmentation fault occurs, or a `ValueError` about mismatched free variable counts is raised.

## Expected Behavior
The autoreload extension should update all function attributes, including closure state, to match the reloaded module. Calling `old_f()` should print the updated closure values (`bx`/`ay`) and return `'v2'` without errors.

## Actual Behavior
- `setattr(old, "__closure__", new.__closure__)` raises `AttributeError('readonly attribute')` in `autoreload.py`, preventing closure updates.
- Mismatched closure states between `__code__` and `__closure__` causes:
  - Segmentation faults during function execution
  - `ValueError('wrapper() requires a code object with X free vars, not Y')` when free variable counts change
- Current workaround uses `ctypes.pythonapi.PyFunction_SetClosure` (CPython-specific) to force closure updates.

## Scope / Affected Areas
- **Files**: `IPython/extensions/autoreload.py` (function update logic)
- **Components**: Autoreload extension, function object attribute management
- **Potential Solutions**:
  - Use CPython API (`PyFunction_SetClosure`) for direct closure updates (current workaround)
  - Implement reference tracking via `gc.get_referrers()` to update all old function references
  - Generate trampoline functions to preserve closure structure (performance tradeoff)
  - Add validation for free variable consistency during reload

AST row select cannot reference edge alias properties after traversal
## Summary
On the AST/GFQL path, row projection can reference node aliases like `friend.firstName`, but it currently fails when projecting an edge alias property such as `r.creationDate` after a traversal.

## Status

**Partially fixed in v0.53.9 (PR #986).**

The **Cypher string path** now works:
```python
g.gfql("MATCH (a)-[r:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN a.id, r.creationDate AS cd, b.firstName")
# → [{'a.id': 'a', 'cd': 123, 'b.firstName': 'Bob'}]
```

The **native AST path** (`rows()` + `select()`) is still broken:
```python
g.gfql([n(name='n'), e_undirected(name='r'), n(name='friend'), rows(),
        select([('cd', 'r.creationDate')])])
# → unsupported token in row expression: 'r'
```

The Cypher fix works via a bindings table that joins edges with node properties. The AST `rows()` path doesn't go through the same bindings table construction — it would need `rows(alias_endpoints=...)` to be wired into the native chain execution, not just the Cypher lowering.

## Minimal repro (AST path — still failing)
```python
import pandas as pd
from graphistry.tests.test_compute import CGFull
from graphistry.compute.ast import n, e_undirected, rows, select

g = CGFull().nodes(
    pd.DataFrame({
        'id': ['a', 'b'],
        'label__Person': [True, True],
        'firstName': ['Alice', 'Bob'],
        'lastName': ['A', 'B'],
    }),
    'id',
).edges(
    pd.DataFrame({
        's': ['a'],
        'd': ['b'],
        'type': ['KNOWS'],
        'creationDate': [123],
    }),
    's',
    'd',
)

steps = [
    n({'id': 'a', 'label__Person': True}, name='n'),
    e_undirected({'type': 'KNOWS'}, name='r'),
    n({'label__Person': True}, name='friend'),
    rows(),
    select([
        ('personId', 'friend.id'),
        ('firstName', 'friend.firstName'),
        ('friendshipCreationDate', 'r.creationDate'),
    ]),
]

print(g.gfql(steps)._nodes)
```

## Observed behavior
```
GFQLTypeError [invalid-node-reference] Error executing 'select': unsupported token in row expression: 'r'
```

## Expected behavior
```python
[{'personId': 'b', 'firstName': 'Bob', 'friendshipCreationDate': 123}]
```

## Likely relation
Depends on wiring `rows(alias_endpoints=...)` into the native AST chain execution path, not just the Cypher lowering path.

Handle ExceptionGroup formatting gracefully (Python 3.11+)
PySnooper formats exceptions using `traceback.format_exception_only(*arg[:2])` and then truncates the result to `max_variable_length`.

Python 3.11 introduced `ExceptionGroup`, and `format_exception_only` produces multi-line nested output for these. When that gets truncated, the result can be confusing or broken mid-line.

We should detect `ExceptionGroup` (on 3.11+) and produce a cleaner single-line summary, something like:

    ExceptionGroup: 'task errors' (3 sub-exceptions: ValueError, TypeError, RuntimeError)

This keeps the output scannable and consistent with how PySnooper handles regular exceptions, while still giving useful info about the group contents.

On older Pythons (including 2.7), nothing changes since `ExceptionGroup` doesn't exist there.

The multi-line nested output gets truncated by PySnooper's `max_variable_length` limit, resulting in confusing or incomplete error messages.

## Expected Behavior
When encountering an `ExceptionGroup`, PySnooper should display a single-line summary format like:

```

```

Summary                                                                         

The compat module in Pint currently eagerly imports optional dependencies       
(including heavy libraries like dask) during initial import, negatively         
impacting performance. This behavior increases startup time for applications    
that use Pint but do not require these optional features. The goal is to        
refactor the import strategy to delay loading these dependencies until they are 
actually needed.                                                                


Steps to Reproduce                                                              

 1 Import Pint in a clean Python environment: import pint                       
 2 Measure the time taken for the import to complete                            
 3 Observe that the compat module imports dask and other optional dependencies  
   immediately during initialization

Optional dependencies (e.g., dask) should only be imported when explicitly      
required (e.g., when handling a dask.array object). This would:                 

 • Reduce initial import time                                                   
 • Avoid unnecessary memory usage for users who don't use optional features     
 • Follow best practices for lazy loading in Python libraries                   


Actual Behavior

optional dependencies during module initialization. For example:                

                                                                                
from dask import array as da  # Eager import (performance bottleneck)

Feature request: improve support for parameter injection
### Why is this needed?

My apologies if there something already exists that addresses this issue. I searched all of the code and I just could not figure out a reusable way to handle parameter injection without rolling my own system. 

Request body and query string parsing as well as other aspects of request parsing are not reusable. For example, a pydantic based parameter injection system can be put in place at some point in the stack to make it more reusable. I've implemented this in a work project using a custom decorator

```python
from functools import wraps
from typing import Optional, Type
import inspect
import json

from aws_lambda_powertools.utilities.data_classes import APIGatewayProxyEvent
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

from lib.common.app import app

# NOTE: this utility does not map these types to the open api specification. 
def inject_params(
    query_model: Optional[Type[BaseModel]] = None,
    body_model: Optional[Type[BaseModel]] = None,
):
    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            _ = args
            api_event: APIGatewayProxyEvent = app.current_event
            query_params = None
            body_params = None

            if query_model:
                query_dict = api_event.query_string_parameters or {}
                try:
                    query_params = query_model(**query_dict)
                except ValidationError as e:
                    # Raise validation error to be handled by existing middleware
                    raise e

            if body_model:
                try:
                    body_dict = json.loads(api_event.body or "{}")
                    body_params = body_model(**body_dict)
                except (ValidationError, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
                    # Raise validation error to be handled by existing middleware
                    raise e

            # Dynamically inject only the parameters that the handler expects
            handler_sig = inspect.signature(func)
            if "query_params" in handler_sig.parameters and query_params is not None:
                kwargs["query_params"] = query_params
            if "body_params" in handler_sig.parameters and body_params is not None:
                kwargs["body_params"] = body_params

            return func(*args, **kwargs)

        return wrapper

    return decorator
```

Example usage:


```python

from http import HTTPStatus

from get_things import get_things
from lib.common.api_client.models.responses import PaginatedThingResponse
from lib.common.app import app, logger, metrics
from lib.common.aws import JsonResponse # custom class I implemented, ignore for the scope of this issue
from lib.common.dtos import GetThingsRequest
from lib.common.middleware.inject_params import inject_params
from lib.common.utils import run_async


@app.get("/thing")
@inject_params(query_model=GetThingsRequest)
def handler(
    query_params: GetThingsRequest,
) -> JsonResponse[PaginatedThingResponse]:
    response: PaginatedThingResponse = run_async(get_things, query_params)
    return JsonResponse(response, status_code=HTTPStatus.OK)
```


So this allows for reusable request parsing with pydantic.  The documented parsing strategy at this time is something that otherwise has to be repeated in every handler. Since this framework really leans into pydantic already I think this kind of functionality should exist. My implementation doesn't cover header parsing or anything else, but it could be extended to support it. 

I'd be happy to make an open source contribution if it makes sense. If so, where would be the best place?

Make ACE lesson matching opt-in via configuration
## Problem

The ACE (Automated Context Embedding) lesson matching system currently auto-enables when it detects that `sentence-transformers` is installed. This causes issues:

1. **Fragile import detection**: The code tries to import `sentence_transformers` and if available, initializes ACE
2. **Silent failures**: When ACE initialization fails (e.g., missing attributes), it logs warnings but falls back silently
3. **Environment confusion**: In pipx environments, dependencies may or may not be available depending on installation method
4. **Not user-controlled**: Users can't explicitly enable/disable ACE

## Current Behavior

From `gptme/tools/lessons.py`:
- Auto-detects `sentence_transformers` availability
- If available, tries to initialize `LessonEmbedder`
- If initialization fails, logs warning and falls through

This causes logs like:
```
Error: sentence-transformers not installed.
WARNING Error during lesson auto-inclusion: 'LessonEmbedder' object has no attribute '_lesson_to_id'
```

## Proposed Solution

Make ACE opt-in via gptme configuration:

```toml
# gptme.toml
[lessons]
ace_enabled = false  # Explicit opt-in
```

Or via environment variable:
```bash
GPTME_ACE_ENABLED=true gptme
```

Benefits:
- User controls whether to use experimental features
- Clear error messages when explicitly enabled but dependencies missing
- No silent failures in production use
- Clean separation between keyword matching (stable) and ACE (experimental)

## Additional Cleanup

The `lessons.py` import detection could use cleanup:
- Remove fragile try/except import pattern
- Add proper configuration check before attempting ACE
- Clear error messages when configuration doesn't match available dependencies

## Context

This came up during autonomous operation health checks - the lesson system was silently failing every run without clear indication of the issue.

cc @ErikBjare

M3 follow-up: tighten unknown-alias MATCH route contract in LogicalPlanner
Context: PR #1155 expanded route coverage and is now merged. During review we noted a non-blocking contract risk that was not addressed in that PR.

## Problem
`LogicalPlanner._reject_unsupported_match_shape()` currently allows planning when no MATCH alias appears in `semantic_table` (`has_known_alias == False`), and `_plan_match()` can emit `PatternMatch` with sparse/empty typed schema. This permissive path is useful for some synthetic constructor flows, but it also broadens `logical_plan_route == "planned"` into shapes that may not have sufficient typed alias context once M3 physical planning starts consuming these plans.

## Why this matters now
M2/M3 route metadata is increasingly used as an execution contract. Overly permissive `planned` classification can hide unsupported shapes that should stay explicitly deferred with a reason.

## Desired behavior
Either:
1. Defer unknown-alias MATCH shapes by default in normal query lowering with explicit `logical_plan_defer_reason`, OR
2. Keep permissive planning only for the specific constructor/synthetic flow that requires it, with explicit gating and regression tests that lock that boundary.

## Acceptance criteria
- Unknown-alias MATCH behavior is explicit and scoped (not broad permissive fallback).
- `logical_plan_route` stays `planned` only for shapes with sufficient planner contract context.
- Add focused tests for:
  - normal query path unknown-alias behavior (planned vs deferred as designed)
  - constructor/synthetic exception path if retained
- Route/defer reasons are stable and explicit for unsupported cases.

## References
- PR #1155: https://github.com/graphistry/pygraphistry/pull/1155
- Review comment: https://github.com/graphistry/pygraphistry/pull/1155#issuecomment-4283501434
- Related lane: #1154

original_text:
segmentation fault with autoreload due to not updating function __closure__
The code for updating old function references in `IPython/extensions/autoreload.py` is fairly straightforward:
```
func_attrs = [
    "__code__",
    "__defaults__",
    "__doc__",
    "__closure__",
    "__globals__",
    "__dict__",
]


def update_function(old, new):
    """Upgrade the code object of a function"""
    for name in func_attrs:
        try:
            setattr(old, name, getattr(new, name))
        except (AttributeError, TypeError):
            pass
```
But calling setattr on `__closure__` gets `AttributeError('readonly attribute')` so it doesn't actually update it.

We have the following code in reload.py:
```
def decorate(func):
    free_var_y = "y"
    free_var_x = "x"

    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("x is:", free_var_x)
        print("y is:", free_var_y)
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


@decorate
def f():
    return "v1"
```

In IPython we do:
```
In [1]: %load_ext autoreload

In [2]: %autoreload all

In [3]: from reload import f

In [4]: old_f = f

In [5]: old_f()
x is: x
y is: y
Out[5]: 'v1'
```

Now we update reload.py to be:
```
def decorate(func):
    free_var_ay = "ay"
    free_var_bx = "bx"

    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("x is:", free_var_bx)
        print("y is:", free_var_ay)
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


@decorate
def f():
    return "v2"
```
Now the co_freevars of the new code object are in a different order from the old function's `__closure__` attribute so I expected IPython to print the wrong values. But actually now when calling old_f or f again in IPython I get a segmentation fault. Also when a function has changed the number of variables it closes over, as IPython updates `__code__` but not `__closure__`, we will get an error like ValueError('wrapper() requires a code object with 3 free vars, not 6').

I am working on an environment to enable interactive development without restarting python using autoreload, where I addressed this in this commit: https://codeberg.org/sczi/swanky-python/commit/748952d0eda733c7abef5e7e01c1dafdc42e4b43

I just use ctypes.pythonapi.PyFunction_SetClosure which is a CPython only api, as I don't currently have a need for supporting pypy or other implementations. I considered some possibilities that should work on all python implementations:
1) find and update old references with gc.get_referrers
If we update all dict references to use the full new function object, that takes care of top level module references by way of `module.__dict__`, local variables by way of frame.f_locals dict, and class instance variables or methods by way of `class.__dict__`. But we would need special cases to handle classes with slots, and references stored in lists or other container types. But we can't include custom checks for every possible container type, just the containers in the standard library, and we can't update old references in immutable containers like tuples. So it would mostly work but cause occasional bugs by not updating everything properly.
2) use a trampoline function
We could generate a trampoline function with the same number of freevars as the old function object, that just wraps and calls the new version. This would avoid the errors about `ValueError('wrapper() requires a code object with 3 free vars, not 6')`. But it requires wrapping functions which would impact performance and pollute stack traces.

functions is not properly updated during autoreload, leading to inconsistencies 
between the function's code object and its closure variables.                   


Reproduction Steps                                                              

 1 Create a file reload.py with this content:                                   

                                                                                
                                                                                
def decorate(func):                                                             
                                                                                
    free_var_y = "y"                                                            
                                                                                
    free_var_x = "x"                                                            
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):                                               
                                                                                
        print("x is:", free_var_x)                                              
                                                                                
        print("y is:", free_var_y)                                              
                                                                                
        return func(*args, **kwargs)                                            
                                                                                
    return wrapper                                                              
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
@decorate                                                                       
                                                                                
def f():                                                                        
                                                                                
    return "v1"                                                                 
                                                                                

 2 In IPython, run:                                                             

                                                                                
                                                                                
In [1]: %load_ext autoreload                                                    
                                                                                
In [2]: %autoreload all                                                         
                                                                                
In [3]: from reload import f                                                    
                                                                                
In [4]: old_f = f                                                               
                                                                                
In [5]: old_f()                                                                 
                                                                                

Output:                                                                         

                                                                                
                                                                                
x is: x                                                                         
                                                                                
y is: y                                                                         
                                                                                
'v1'                                                                            
                                                                                

 3 Modify reload.py to change closure variable names and return value:          

                                                                                
                                                                                
def decorate(func):                                                             
                                                                                
    free_var_ay = "ay"                                                          
                                                                                
    free_var_bx = "bx"                                                          
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):                                               
                                                                                
        print("x is:", free_var_bx)                                             
                                                                                
        print("y is:", free_var_ay)                                             
                                                                                
        return func(*args, **kwargs)                                            
                                                                                
    return wrapper                                                              
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
@decorate                                                                       
                                                                                
def f():                                                                        
                                                                                
    return "v2"                                                                 
                                                                                

 4 In IPython, run:                                                             

                                                                                
                                                                                
In [6]: old_f()                                                                 
                                                                                

Result: Segmentation fault or ValueError('wrapper() requires a code object with 
3 free vars, not 6')                                                            


Expected vs Actual Behavior                                                     

Expected:                                                                       

After reloading, calling old_f() should display the updated closure variables   
("bx" and "ay") and return "v2".                                                

Actual:                                                                         

 • Segmentation fault occurs when calling old_f() after reload                  
 • Or ValueError when the number of closure variables changes between reloads   


Root Cause Analysis                                                             

The autoreload implementation in IPython/extensions/autoreload.py attempts to   
update function attributes with this code:                                      

                                                                                
                                                                                
func_attrs = [                                                                  
                                                                                
    "__code__",                                                                 
                                                                                
    "__defaults__",                                                             
                                                                                
    "__doc__",                                                                  
                                                                                
    "__closure__",                                                              
                                                                                
    "__globals__",                                                              
                                                                                
    "__dict__",                                                                 
                                                                                
]                                                                               
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
def update_function(old, new):                                                  
                                                                                
    for name in func_attrs:                                                     
                                                                                
        try:                                                                    
                                                                                
            setattr(old, name, getattr(new, name))                              
                                                                                
        except (AttributeError, TypeError):                                     
                                                                                
            pass                                                                
                                                                                

However, __closure__ is a read-only attribute in CPython, causing setattr(old,  
"__closure__", ...) to fail silently. This leaves the function's closure in an  
inconsistent state with its updated code object.                                


Proposed Solutions                                                              

 1 CPython-specific fix (implemented in this commit):                           
    • Use ctypes.pythonapi.PyFunction_SetClosure to directly set the closure    
    • Works only on CPython implementations                                     
 2 Cross-implementation solution:                                               
    • Use gc.get_referrers() to find and update all references to the old       
      function                                                                  
    • Challenges:                                                               
       • Requires special handling for classes with slots                       
       • Cannot update references in immutable containers (e.g., tuples)        
       • May miss custom container implementations                              
 3 Trampoline function approach:                                                
    • Create wrapper functions with matching closure signatures                 
    • Performance impact and stack trace pollution                              


Environment Details                                                             

 • CPython 3.x (exact version may vary)                                         
 • IPython 8.x (autoreload extension)                                           
 • Reproducible in both Linux and macOS environments                            


Files Involved                                                                  

 • IPython/extensions/autoreload.py (contains the update_function               
   implementation)                                                              
 • User code files using decorated functions with closures (e.g., reload.py in  
   the example)

fix: custom macro parameters not expanded in LaTeX backend
## Description

The LaTeX backend does not expand custom macro parameters (`#1`, `#2`, etc.) when processing user-defined macros via `\newcommand`. This causes unexpanded parameter references and their surrounding formatting commands to leak into the output.

**Example:**
```latex
\newcommand{\highlight}[1]{\textcolor{white}{\textbf{#1}}}
\highlight{Result}
```
produces output containing literal `\textcolor{white}{\textbf{#1}}` or `\textbf{#1}` instead of the substituted text "Result".

Another pattern:
```latex
\newcommand{\metric}[2]{#1{\scriptsize$\_{#2}$}}
```
leaks `\scriptsize` and `#2` references.

## Affected Papers (from testing on 24 arXiv papers)

| Paper | Leaked Commands | Count |
|-------|----------------|-------|
| 2603.25737v1 | `\textbf`, `\small` | 35+12 |
| 2603.25723v1 | `\scriptsize` | 12 |

## Root Cause

When `\newcommand` definitions are encountered, the backend stores the macro body but does not substitute `#1`/`#2`/etc. with actual arguments at expansion time.

## Expected Behavior

Custom macro parameters should be properly substituted with their arguments before the macro body is parsed for formatting commands.

## Context

Discovered during extended testing for PR #3204. See [test report comment](https://github.com/docling-project/docling/pull/3204#issuecomment) for full details.

Defining units without a default results in unexpected NaNs
According to the [online docs](https://pint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/contexts.html#working-without-a-default-definition):

> In some cases, the definition of a certain unit may be so volatile to make it unwise to define a default conversion rate in the UnitRegistry.
> 
> This can be solved by using ‘NaN’ (any capitalization) instead of a conversion rate rate in the UnitRegistry, and then override it in contexts:
> 
> ```python
> truckload = nan kg
> 
> @context Euro_TIR
>     truckload = 2000 kg
> @end
> 
> @context British_grocer
>     truckload = 500 lb
> @end
> ```
> 
> This allows you, before any context is activated, to define quantities and perform dimensional analysis:
> 
> ```python
> >>> ureg.truckload.dimensionality
> [mass]
> >>> q = ureg.Quantity("2 truckloads")
> >>> q.to("kg")
> nan kg
> >>> q.to("kg", "Euro_TIR")
> 4000 kilogram
> >>> q.to("kg", "British_grocer")
> 453.59237 kilogram
> ```

Based on that, I would have naturally assumed that

```python
>>> ureg.Quantity("1000 truckloads").to("kilotruckload")
```
would yield
```python
1 kilotruckload
```
but instead it yields
```python
nan kilotruckload
```

Could this be fixed?
